steps.line: In the Upanishads, ancient Hindu teachings, King Janaka once offered a thousand cows, gold tied to their horns, to the wisest teacher in his court.
The sage Yajnavalkya calmly told his student to lead the cows home. The other scholars were not pleased. One by one, they stood up to question him.
Artabhaga asked the biggest question of all: when a person dies, and their breath and sight and speech return to nature, what becomes of that person?

steps.q: Yajnavalkya takes Artabhaga aside to answer in private. What do you think they talk about?
o: The gods who take the dead
steps.why: Action. Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.2.13: what they talked about was karma, and what they praised was karma.

steps.line: Take my hand, my friend, said Yajnavalkya. This is not for a crowd. Only the two of us should know. And they walked away together.

steps.q: Why would Yajnavalkya refuse to answer in front of everyone?
o: He didn’t know, and wanted to hide it
It was for a seeker, not a scoreboard
He was dodging, to keep the cows
steps.why: The text doesn’t say why. Many readers think karma was then a new, deep teaching, shared quietly with one serious seeker.

steps.line: What did they talk about? Action. Karma. What they praised was action: a person becomes good by good action, and bad by bad action.

steps.q: In the older Vedic texts, the word karma usually meant one kind of action in particular. What kind?
steps.why: Karma meant ritual work, done right. In this Upanishad it widens to every deed you do, and what it makes of you.

steps.line: Today, “instant karma” means someone else getting what’s coming. The old word turns you around: what am I becoming, with this choice?
steps.label: today

steps.q: Among the scholars who stood to question Yajnavalkya in that court was one woman. Who?
steps.why: Gargi Vachaknavi questioned him twice, pressing all the way to what the whole world is woven on. Maitreyi, the other famous woman, was his wife.

say: here’s what i love. in hindu teaching, karma starts deeper than the deed. later, the same upanishad says it: as your desire, so your will. as your will, so your deed. as your deed, so you become.
so the intention is the seed. in this teaching, karma isn’t a scoreboard for other people. it’s what you’re growing in yourself.

steps.q: Someone cuts in line and then spills their coffee. “Instant karma!” says your friend. What would Yajnavalkya’s answer turn you toward?
o: Trusting the universe to even the score
Asking what that person did to deserve it
What your own reaction is planting in you
steps.why: His answer was about what each of us becomes by what we do. The only karma in that moment you can tend is yours.

today.say: pick one choice you’ll make today: a reply, a tone of voice, a small favor. before you make it, notice the intention under it. choose the seed.

Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 3.2.13: Artabhaga asks what becomes of a person when speech goes into fire, breath into wind, eye into the sun, and so on; Yajnavalkya: “Take my hand, my friend. We two alone shall know of this; this is not for us two in public.” They went aside; what they spoke of was karma, what they praised was karma: one becomes good by good action, bad by bad action. Trans. Patrick Olivelle, Upanisads (Oxford World’s Classics, 1996).
Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 4.4.5: as is a person’s desire, so is their resolve (will); as their resolve, so their deed.
